# Finite global cuts realize sums of physical boundary speeds

This note proves a closure theorem for ACTUAL compatible deformations.
It is not Minkowski interpolation of the deformed bodies. It combines
the supporting planes and convex cut fields before forming a new
ambient intersection. The resulting first inward speeds, total losses,
and every fixed closed-cap loss are the prescribed nonnegative linear
combinations of those of the original deformations.

No payment inequality, parity cost bound, or exchange of critical-menu
and supporting-allocation quantifiers is asserted. The theorem concerns
the finite global supporting-cut class, rather than every conceivable
compatible deformation.

IMPORTANT SCOPE ADDITION: Sections 7--9 prove that every speed in this
class is an L1 boundary limit of the archived convex normal-roof
variations, in fact using ONE normal-independent convex potential at
each approximation stage. Thus the exact construction is new as a
realization of summed speeds, but it adds no strict finite-response
separation power beyond that archived potential cone. Neutral/equality
responses are not automatically realized by the approximating fields.

Dependencies are the continuous support-slope lemma and the radial
first-variation proof in
`candidate 6748c967393345b9`.
We restate the needed hypotheses and give the actual construction and
first-variation argument below. The contrast with body interpolation
is the exact example in
`candidate d9792f1ce8a8f405`.

## 1. The common original family and the allowed actions

Let d>=1. Let P be a nonempty finite set in Z^n such that

    conv(P) intersect Z^n = P.

For each z in P let K_z be a full-dimensional compact convex body in
R^d. Assume every actual anchored inclusion

    sum_z lambda_z K_z subset K_q,
    lambda_z>=0, sum lambda_z=1, sum lambda_z z=q in P.       (1)

Consequently the relative convex hull

    C=conv union_(z in P) ({z} times K_z)

has precisely the specified integer fibers. Write h_z(u)=h_(K_z)(u)
for unit continuous normal u in S^(d-1).

There are N>=1 actions. Action a has a nonempty finite index set I_a.
For i in I_a it has:

* a plane ell_ai(u,z), continuous in u and affine in the real base z;
* a field V_ai(u,z,x), continuous in all variables and nonnegative,
  whose dependence on (z,x) is convex for each fixed u;
* the support-majorant property

      ell_ai(u,z)>=h_z(u) for every z in P and u.            (2)

Joint continuity on the relevant compact sets suffices; the fields may
be defined on all of aff(P) times R^d. No projective form is required.
The projective fields of the cited source are instances of these
hypotheses, with distinct sources, slopes, and base shifts allowed.

The actual action is

    C_a(e)=C intersect
       { (z,x): u.x+e V_ai(u,z,x)<=ell_ai(u,z)
                         for every i in I_a and every u }.       (3)

The planes in (2) majorize u.x on ALL of C: this follows by applying
their affine dependence on z to a convex representation by original
fiber points. Thus C_a(0)=C. Each C_a(e) is convex and nested as e
increases. Section 4 proves a common inner-homothet estimate, so these
families retain positive fibers and the original projection for small e.

Set Delta_ai,z(u)=ell_ai(u,z)-h_z(u)>=0. At a regular boundary point
x of K_z, with its unique outward unit normal u_z(x), the old action
has first inward speed

    v_az(x)=max( { V_ai(u_z(x),z,x):
                         Delta_ai,z(u_z(x))=0 } union {0} ).     (4)

All assertions about boundary speeds are surface-almost everywhere.
This includes d=1, where boundary measure is H_0 on the two endpoints.

## 2. Zero augmentation supplies active planes everywhere

For every p in P choose a bounded continuous support slope A_p(u) with

    h_z(u)<=h_p(u)+A_p(u).(z-p),       z in P.              (5)

Existence follows from (1) by finite Farkas duality. Continuity can be
obtained by the minimum-norm feasible selection: the fixed constraint
matrix has finitely many independent active-row formulas, so sequential
continuity follows from feasibility and the projection optimality
conditions. The full elementary argument is in the cited source.

To EVERY action add, for each p, the plane and field

    ell_0p(u,z)=h_p(u)+A_p(u).(z-p),    V_0p=0.             (6)

These cuts are redundant on C for every e. Hence augmentation changes
neither the actual family (3) nor its speed (4). For every z and u,
however, the augmented action now has an active plane: choose p=z.
Accordingly (4) is the ordinary maximum over a NONEMPTY finite active
set, without needing the auxiliary union with {0}.

This augmentation is necessary for the following product construction:
one original action can have no active nonzero cut at a given boundary
point, while another does. Its zero speed must remain an available
choice there.

## 3. The product-of-planes construction

Fix any desired coefficients t_1,...,t_N>=0. Independently choose
strictly positive baseline weights rho_a>0 with sum rho_a=1. They can
be fixed once, for example rho_a=1/N, even if some t_a=0.

For every tuple i=(i_1,...,i_N) from the AUGMENTED index sets put

    ell_i(u,z)=sum_a rho_a ell_(a i_a)(u,z),
    V_i(u,z,x)=sum_a t_a V_(a i_a)(u,z,x).                 (7)

Define the new actual family by

    C_t(e)=C intersect
       { (z,x): u.x+e V_i(u,z,x)<=ell_i(u,z)
                       for every tuple i and every u }.        (8)

There are finitely many tuples. The new plane is affine in z and
majorizes the original fiber support. The new field is continuous,
nonnegative and convex in the full physical variables. Thus (8) is an
actual nested ambient convex intersection of the same class as (3).

Its slack at an original fiber is

    Delta_i,z(u)=sum_a rho_a Delta_(a i_a),z(u).           (9)

Every summand is nonnegative and every rho_a is positive. Therefore

    Delta_i,z(u)=0  iff  Delta_(a i_a),z(u)=0 for EVERY a. (10)

The choices of active indices in (10) are independent and their sets
are nonempty by zero augmentation. Maximizing the new field gives

    max_(active tuples) sum_a t_a V_(a i_a)(u,z,x)
       =sum_a t_a max_(active i_a) V_(a i_a)(u,z,x).       (11)

The actual physical speed of (8) is consequently

                       v_tz(x)=sum_a t_a v_az(x).        (12)

This is an equality of speeds at the SAME original physical boundary
point and normal. There is no optimization over pairs of different
points on a flat face. That distinction is exactly what fails for
Minkowski interpolation of deformed bodies.

Using positive baseline weights independent of t is important.
Omitting an action merely because its desired coefficient is zero is
unnecessary, and letting a baseline weight vanish would destroy the
equivalence (10). No bound on the slopes of a limiting sequence of
actions is used: N and all actions in this theorem are fixed and finite.

## 4. Positivity, exact compatibility, and the first-variation proof

Choose o_z+r_z B subset K_z with r_z>0, for every z in P. The finite
tuple fields and compact normal sphere have a common upper bound M on
the finitely many original fibers. For tau=e M/r_z and small e, every
point of

    o_z+(1-tau)(K_z-o_z)

satisfies all cuts in (8). Indeed its original support slack in each
unit direction is at least tau r_z=e M, while the additional baseline
slack is nonnegative. The field remains at most M on this inner body.
If M=0 there is no motion. This proves uniformly O(e) inward movement,
positive d-volume at every original base, and exact projection
conv(P). Since (8) is convex, all its integer fibers satisfy (1)
exactly. Lattice completeness excludes any new integer bases.

For completeness, fix a regular old boundary point x of K_z. On its
ray from o_z write x_s=o_z+(1-s)(x-o_z), and let s_e be the fractional
radial loss to the new endpoint. The inner-homothet bound gives
0<=s_e<=O(e) uniformly. For every OLD active cut at x,

    s_e u.(x-o_z) >= e V_i(u,z,x_(s_e)).                  (13)

At a regular x all supporting normals equal u_z(x), and
u_z(x).(x-o_z)>=r_z. Taking a lower limit gives the maximum of the
active field values divided by this radial denominator.

For the reverse bound, whenever s_e>0 the new endpoint is in the old
interior, so at least one new cut is active. There are finitely many
tuples and a compact normal sphere. Along a subsequence its tuple and
normal converge. The active equality implies that the old slack

    h_z(u)-u.x+Delta_i,z(u)

is O(e). Both terms are nonnegative, so the limit normal supports x
and its tuple has zero original slack. In the active equality,
discarding this nonnegative old slack gives the matching upper bound
for s_e/e. Hence

    s_e/e -> v_tz(x)/[u_z(x).(x-o_z)].                   (14)

This also explains why cross-normal effects cannot create another
first speed at a regular point. Normals of new active constraints must
converge to its UNIQUE old normal. Nonsmooth points form a set of
surface measure zero. No continuity of the active-contact indicator is
assumed.

The radial Jacobian is u_z(x).(x-o_z). Dominated convergence, using
the uniform O(e) estimate, proves

    |K_z|-|C_t(e)_z|
       =e integral_(boundary K_z) v_tz dS+o(e).          (15)

In d=1 the same argument is applied directly to the two interval
endpoints. If aff(P) has deficient rank, C_t(e) is a relative convex
body. Adding a fixed sufficiently small ball in the rational
perpendicular base space makes it full-dimensional without introducing
new integer fibers: the perpendicular projection of Z^n is discrete,
and the radius is chosen below its least nonzero norm. This optional
rank repair preserves nesting and every mixed measure in this note;
containment in a previously supplied full-dimensional ambient body is
not asserted.

## 5. Exact addition of every fixed closed-cap response

Let H be any fixed ambient closed halfspace. On boundary K_z use its
ACTUAL inward-loss selector kappa_(z,H):

* it is 1 if the whole fiber is captured, including an inside support
  cut and a closed purely integer cut on the base hyperplane;
* it is 0 if the fiber interior is disjoint from H, including an
  outside supporting trace;
* for a proper continuous cut, it is 1_(interior H_z) on the boundary.

For a proper cut its cutting hyperplane meets the boundary in surface
measure zero. Along each remaining old radial boundary point, the
shrinking layer is eventually wholly on one fixed side. The same
radial dominated convergence gives

    mu(H)-mu_t,e(H)
      =e sum_z integral kappa_(z,H) v_tz dS+o(e).         (16)

For d=1 a proper cut is interior to the interval and misses its two
endpoints, so the same assertion holds. Supporting traces are treated
by the first two cases, never by a fictitious closed-face indicator.

For action a define

    D_a=sum_z integral v_az dS,
    L_a(H)=sum_z integral kappa_(z,H) v_az dS.

Equations (12), (15), and (16) prove, for the new ACTUAL family,

    D_t=sum_a t_a D_a,
    L_t(H)=sum_a t_a L_a(H),                              (17)

simultaneously for every fixed H. A finite chosen menu has uniform
little-o errors. In particular, for any original normalized level
beta and any finite fixed cap list H_j, its response vector satisfies

    L_t(H_j)-beta D_t
       =sum_a t_a [L_a(H_j)-beta D_a].                   (18)

Thus the set of such finite response vectors from finite global-cut
actions is closed under finite nonnegative linear combinations. The
same is true for the speed arrays themselves, modulo surface-null
sets. Convex combinations are the case sum t_a=1. This is algebraic
cone closure; topological closedness of all obtainable arrays or
response vectors is NOT claimed.

## 6. What this does and does not give for a critical menu

If a FINITE fixed cap cover has common critical mass Q and the other
rows have strict slack, an actual combined action with

    L_t(H_j)-beta D_t>0

on every critical row supplies the usual strict normalized cover
decrease. This conclusion retains the hypotheses that the displayed
fixed caps cover all candidate fibers and that their strict slack
persists; cone closure does not produce such a cover or inequality.

There is a separate limitation for MOVING caps. At a supporting facet,
the directional cap derivative involving boundary speed and cap motion
contains minimum/maximum branch expressions. Those expressions need
not add when two independent cap motions are averaged. The present
theorem adds actual BODY speeds and fixed-cap losses. It therefore
also adds any response expression that is linear in that body speed
for one FIXED admissible allocation. It does not exchange the order of
menu selection, supporting allocation, and direction selection. The
quantifiers of
`candidate 07dbcd642c33993d`
must still be
checked at that separate interface.

Prescribed source projective fields from different actions need not
remain exact finite-parameter erosions on their old source fibers.
What is exact is their first-speed sum (12), so their proved seed
credits add with their prescribed coefficients. No larger final source
cost may silently replace a seed cost in a Gamma_d lower bound.

The square calibration in the Minkowski-interpolation source is
consistent with this theorem: top-facet speeds 1+x and 1-x have average
1, realized by the roof 1-e, whereas the half-Minkowski body has roof
1-e|x|. The new construction realizes the former kind of physical
speed addition. It does not reinterpret the latter body's losses.

The additional mechanism is therefore precise: finite global
supporting-cut deformations admit actual nonnegative speed addition,
even with different sources and different original contact sets. It
uses product tuples of supporting planes and positive baseline
averaging, and requires neither smooth boundary nor an unproved
tangent-cone realization argument.

## 7. One global convex potential approximates each contact-max speed

Fix ONE finite global-cut action from Sections 1--3, including, if
needed, a combined action (8). Write its data as ell_i(u,z), V_i(u,z,x).
Zero augmentation may be retained. Define on the full physical space

    g_i(u,z,x)=ell_i(u,z)-u.x,
    Phi_m(z,x)=max_(i,u) [V_i(u,z,x)-m g_i(u,z,x)]_+,
                                                        m>=0. (19)

Here i ranges over a finite set and u over the compact unit sphere.
The important strengthening is that Phi_m has NO remaining normal
argument. It is one ordinary convex potential in (z,x).

For fixed i,u, the gap g_i is affine in (z,x), so each bracket in (19)
is convex; taking its positive part and their supremum preserves
convexity. All indexed functions are jointly continuous, with a compact
index set. Their maxima are finite and continuous on physical space
(on each compact physical set, uniform continuity gives the elementary
maximum-continuity proof). Thus Phi_m is a globally finite, continuous,
nonnegative convex function.

Every original point (z,x) of C has g_i(u,z,x)>=0, by the support-plane
majorant property. Hence on C,

    0<=Phi_(m+1)<=Phi_m<=B,
    B=max_(i,u,(z,x) in C) V_i(u,z,x)<infinity.           (20)

At a regular boundary point x of an integer fiber K_z, write u_0 for
its unique outward normal and v_z(x) for the contact-max speed (4).
Every old active cut at u_0 occurs in (19) with zero gap, so
Phi_m(z,x)>=v_z(x). If the decreasing limit is positive, take maximizers
(i_m,u_m) and a subsequence with fixed i and u_m converging to u_*.
Positive maximal values and (20) imply

    0<=g_i(u_m,z,x)<=B/m.

The limiting gap is zero. Its exact decomposition is

    g_i(u_*,z,x)
      =[ell_i(u_*,z)-h_z(u_*)]+[h_z(u_*)-u_*.x],        (21)

with BOTH summands nonnegative. Therefore the limiting cut has zero
base support slack, and u_* supports K_z at x. Regularity forces
u_*=u_0. Since Phi_m(z,x)<=V_i(u_m,z,x) along these maximizers,
continuity gives an upper limit at most V_i(u_0,z,x)<=v_z(x).
If the decreasing limit is zero, the lower bound already gives
v_z(x)=0. In all cases,

                     Phi_m(z,x) decreases to v_z(x)     (22)

at surface-almost every original fiber boundary point. The proof does
not assert (22) at nonregular points; their possible multiple limiting
normals have zero surface measure. For d=1 each of the two endpoints
has its unique outward normal, and the same compact-index argument
is immediate on S^0.

Let eta be the original finite normal-bundle measure

    integral F d eta
      =sum_z integral_(boundary K_z) F(u_z(x),z,x) dS.

Equations (20)--(22) and dominated convergence give

    ||Phi_m-v||_(L1(eta)) ->0.                          (23)

This is a genuine simultaneous approximation at every measured fiber.
No exposed-contact indicator is assumed continuous, and no uniform
positive support gap away from the contact set is needed.

The simpler normal-dependent expression

    max_i [V_i(u,z,x)-m g_i(u,z,x)]_+

also has (22)--(23) on the normal bundle. The global maximum (19) is
preferable: it belongs literally to the archived finite cone with
one convex physical function and normal weight identically 1, without
an additional partition-of-unity approximation on the normal sphere.

## 8. Actual canonical normal-roof realization and the limit order

For real z in conv(P), let h_C(z,u) be the support of the actual
continuous fiber C_z. Its exact finite-hull formula is

    h_C(z,u)=max{ sum_p alpha_p h_p(u):
       alpha_p>=0, sum alpha_p=1, sum alpha_p p=z }.      (24)

It is jointly continuous, concave in z and continuous piecewise affine
in z for fixed u. These are the finite support-LP properties proved in
Section 1 of `candidate a68c14b477a24d06`.
At integer z in P it equals h_z(u).

For a FIXED finite m define

    C_(m,e)={ (z,x): z in conv(P),
       u.x+e Phi_m(z,x)<=h_C(z,u) for EVERY unit u }.     (25)

Each defining inequality is convex in (z,x), since Phi_m is convex and
h_C is concave in z. Joint continuity makes the set closed. Because
Phi_m>=0, (25) lies in C and is compact and nested as e grows. It has
the SAME positive integer fibers and projection as C for small e:
the inner-homothet argument of Section 4 applies with the bound B in
(20), which is even independent of m on C. The optional rational
perpendicular rank repair is unchanged. Thus (25) is an actual
compatible convex-body deformation, exactly of the old normal-roof
type, not a formal boundary prescription.

For each fixed m, the radial proof of Section 4 applied to (25) gives
the boundary speed Phi_m(z,x). In particular, if D_m and L_m(H) are
its total and fixed closed-cap first losses, then

    D_m=integral Phi_m d eta,
    L_m(H)=integral kappa_H Phi_m d eta.                (26)

The selectors kappa_H are exactly those in Section 5, including inside
support, outside support, and closed purely integer cases. Consequently

    D_m decreases to D,
    L_m(H) decreases to L(H).                           (27)

Signed normalized responses L_m(H)-beta D_m converge to the desired
ones, but need not be monotone. More generally, for every fixed bounded
Borel normal-bundle weight w,

    integral w Phi_m d eta -> integral w v d eta.        (28)

The error is at most ||w||_infinity ||Phi_m-v||_1. Thus convergence is
uniform for any prescribed family of weights with a common finite
supremum bound. This includes finite cap lists, fixed supporting-facet
allocation densities, and fixed continuous affine-hinge weights on the
compact normal bundle. For an ordinary continuous physical weight
w(z,x), including a fixed affine positive-part hinge, the actual loss
of integral w d mu under (25) has derivative integral w Phi_m d eta:
the same radial argument applies with its continuous bounded weight.
Normal-dependent weights in (28) are boundary response functionals;
no unintroduced interior-normal integral is being asserted.

The order of limits is essential. First take e to zero with m FIXED
to obtain (26); then use (23) to compare those first responses as m
increases. For a construction with a strict finite response margin,
choose a sufficiently large FINITE m first, and only then choose e
sufficiently small for that one actual family's first variations.
There is no claim of a little-o remainder uniform in m, or that an
arbitrary simultaneous choice m=m(e) retains these derivatives.

## 9. Exact scope: no additional strict dual power

Suppose a finite fixed cap cover and an action have strict normalized
response margin

    L(H_j)-beta D>=delta>0 for every critical row j.

By (23), (26), and the bound following (28), the same rows of (25)
have margin at least delta/2 for some finite m. Choosing e small after
that m realizes the same strict cover improvement by ONE old convex
physical potential. Finite strict inequalities formed from the other
fixed bounded response weights have the same property. A genuinely
uniform strict inequality over a uniformly bounded allocation family
also persists by the uniform bound after (28); mere pointwise
strictness is not substituted for such a uniform margin.

Conversely, any old continuous nonnegative normal-roof potential
Psi(u,z,x), convex in (z,x) for each u, has its boundary speed realized
by a finite global-cut action: use the supporting planes (6) for every
p and assign the SAME field Psi to each plane. At each (z,u) at least
the p=z plane is active, and every active field equals Psi. Formula
(4) therefore gives exactly Psi(u_z(x),z,x). In particular this applies
to the literal old finite cone of nonnegative sums
sum_l psi_l(u) Phi_l(z,x), with continuous psi_l>=0 and nonnegative
continuous convex Phi_l.

Indeed this converse preserves the entire measured fibers, not just
their first speeds: at each original z, min_p ell_0p(u,z)=h_z(u), so
all the identical-field support-plane cuts are equivalent on that
fiber to its canonical normal-roof inequalities. This is not an
assertion that the two ambient bodies agree between integer bases.

It follows that the L1(eta) closure of the inward finite global-cut
speed class equals the L1(eta) closure of that old finite potential
class: (19)--(23) prove one inclusion, and the preceding explicit
construction proves the other. The old stress theorem additionally
permits signed affine variations; nothing here removes those.

Therefore finite speed addition is a useful exact realization theorem,
but it does NOT strengthen the separating inequalities of a dual
stress already tested against all old convex potentials. The explicit
product-plane construction avoids approximation and retains exact
first responses; it does not furnish a previously missing strict
descent direction relative to that fully quantified cone.

Equality and neutral faces require separate care. Although every
nonnegative loss in (27) decreases to its target, the differences
L_m(H)-beta D_m can approach zero from either sign, and the approximation
need not preserve a response required to equal zero. Neither exact
membership in a neutral response face nor a contact simplification
follows from the L1 closure statement. This is precisely the distinction
between the constructive addition theorem and its lack of new strict
finite-response dual power.

The independent companion
`candidate 61c2a6c203bcade2`
proves the same global-penalty closure and gives explicit examples
illustrating the neutral-response and exact-trace cautions. The present
argument does not need those examples or a claim that the two exact
finite-response sets differ.
